extracted_data.name_full: Application of different calibration methods for the Hargreaves-Samani model in Southeast Brazil
extracted_data.brief_description: Case study comparing several approaches to estimate reference evapotranspiration (ET0) using temperature-based methods and Penman-Monteith (PM) as reference, including evaluation of the FAO-56 limited-data assumption that dew point ≈ Tmin, regional HC parameterizations, and a global linear regression correction.
extracted_data.study_region: State of Espírito Santo, southeast Brazil (approx. lat 17°52'–21°19' S, lon 39°38'–41°50' W); 17 weather stations (9 inside state + 8 neighboring), elevations ~9–976 m; daily observations 2009–2013.
extracted_data.climate_zone_context: Mixed climates within the state: Aw (tropical savanna with dry season), Am (monsoon), Cfa/Cfb/Cwa/Cwb (temperate/humid variants) per Köppen; mean annual precipitation 1,000–1,600 mm and mean annual temperature 18–24 °C; study explicitly contrasts drier (e.g., Linhares, Aw) vs humid/mountainous sites (e.g., Caparaó, Cwb).
extracted_data.target_variable_definition: Primary modeled quantity in study is reference evapotranspiration ET0. For FAO-56 limited-data (PML) application the actual vapour pressure e_a is estimated by computing dew point temperature T_dew from Tmin (i.e., assuming T_dew ≈ Tmin) using Tetens' equation; study does not directly reconstruct specific humidity or VPD but the e_a/T_dew assumption is central to PML.
extracted_data.predictors_used: Predictors used across methods: daily Tmin (primary predictor for dew point/e_a in PML), Tmax, Tmean, diurnal temperature range ΔT (Tmax–Tmin), extraterrestrial radiation R_a (and Hargreaves Rs proxy), station latitude/longitude/altitude for regional HC models; when PM used as reference it used full meteorological inputs (radiation, RH, wind) available from INMET. For PML, wind speed is substituted with a constant 2 m s⁻¹ and Rs estimated with Hargreaves temperature-based equation (kRs).
extracted_data.fao56_assumption_details: FAO-56 limited-data procedure implemented: assume dew point temperature T_po ≈ Tmin at sunrise so actual vapor pressure e_a computed from Tmin via Tetens' formula; assume wind speed = 2 m s⁻¹ if missing; estimate Rs with Hargreaves equation R_s = k_Rs R_a sqrt(Tmax - Tmin) with k_Rs = 0.16 (interior) or 0.19 (coastal) per FAO guidance. Study reports that applying these FAO-56 limited-data assumptions (PML) produced the worst ET0 performance (large positive bias) in this region.
extracted_data.model_family: Empirical temperature-based models and linear regressions: Hargreaves-Samani original empirical formula; HC (Hargreaves coefficient) regionalization via simple linear regression forms (Vanderlinden-style: HC = k1 * Tmean/ΔT + k2) and multiple linear regression (Martí-style) using Tmean, ΔT and geographic variables; global/simple linear calibration ET0 = a + b * ET0_HS (ordinary least squares). No machine learning (RF/NN) or AR time-series models were used in this study.
extracted_data.localization_strategy: Local and regional strategies tested: (a) per-station mean HC computed from daily HC then a regional regression across stations (Vanderlinden approach); (b) regional multiple linear regression of mean station HC on Tmean, ΔT and coordinates/altitude (Martí approach) to get regional HC; (c) global linear regression (ET0_PM vs ET0_HS) fit using all stations, with leave-one-out cross-validation applied when evaluating station performance to avoid bias. The HC adjustments are regional (fit across stations) while the linear ET0 correction was evaluated with cross-station validation.
extracted_data.seasonality_handling: No explicit day-of-year or monthly models were used; HC regressions were built from mean station HC values (averaged over the 5-year period), and the ET0 linear correction was fitted on daily data pooled across the full period (no DOY-specific coefficients). The study notes but does not implement per-day calibrated approaches (refers to Zanetti et al. 2019 as a promising per-condition calibration).
extracted_data.day_of_year_window: Not used — study did not apply explicit DOY-window smoothing or monthly bins; HC was averaged per station over the full record and regressions used those station means; linear regression calibration used daily pooled data (no DOY window).
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: None reported — anomalies (departure from climatology) were not defined or used in the tested methods.
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lagged_terms: None — no lagged dew point/ea or autoregressive predictors were included in any tested method.
extracted_data.physical_mechanisms_for_skill: Mechanistic rationale reported/discussed: FAO-56 assumption relies on near-saturated conditions at sunrise so Tmin approximates dew point (Tdew≈Tmin); Hargreaves methods exploit diurnal temperature range as a proxy for radiation/clear-sky conditions (larger ΔT indicates more insolation and higher ET0); regional differences (humidity, cloudiness, coastal influence) change the Tmin–Tdew relationship and thereby HC, explaining why local/regional calibration improves skill; also climate homogeneity (as in southern Spain) yields better HC parameter fits than heterogeneous regions like Espírito Santo.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling: Implicit interpretation: study pooled daily data across seasons and stations to fit regional HC and global ET0 correction, noting that pooled/regional fits perform worse where climate heterogeneity is larger (they attribute Vanderlinden's stronger fit in Spain to climate homogeneity). The paper does not explicitly test or recommend wide DOY windows; instead it suggests that per-day/condition calibration might improve performance.
extracted_data.validation_data_sources: Ground truth: Penman-Monteith (FAO-56) ET0 computed using full INMET station data (where available) used as the reference. Input/validation stations: INMET network (17 stations total: 9 in ES + 8 neighboring), daily Tmax, Tmin, global solar radiation, relative humidity and wind speed for 2009–2013; days with data failures were discarded. Quality control: authors used previously-processed dataset from Xavier et al. (2015) and removed days with failures.
extracted_data.performance_metrics: Reported metrics: MAE, MBE (bias), RMSE, RRMSE (relative RMSE), and r² between estimated ET0 and PM reference. Key aggregated results (all stations combined): Hargreaves-Samani (original) MAE=0.68 mm day⁻¹, MBE=0.47, RMSE=0.83, RRMSE=0.22, r²=0.78; PML (FAO-56 limited-data) MAE=1.46, MBE=1.43, RMSE=1.63, RRMSE=0.44, r²=0.73; Martí et al. (HC regression) MAE=0.81, MBE=-0.18, RMSE=1.01, RRMSE=0.27, r²=0.54; Vanderlinden et al. (HC regression) MAE=0.77, MBE=0.17, RMSE=1.00, RRMSE=0.27, r²=0.54; Linear regression correction MAE=0.53, MBE≈0.00, RMSE=0.68, RRMSE=0.18, r²=0.78. Site-level best/worst per-method statistics are listed in Table 4.
extracted_data.comparators_and_baselines: Baselines compared: Penman-Monteith with full data (reference), Penman-Monteith limited-data (PML) using FAO-56 assumptions, Hargreaves-Samani original, HC-adjusted HS (Vanderlinden and Martí formulations), and a global linear regression correction. Quantitatively, PML performed worst (large bias MAE~1.46 mm day⁻¹), linear regression correction performed best (reduced MAE by up to ~30% vs original HS).
extracted_data.reported_failure_modes: Reported failure modes: PML (FAO-56 limited-data with Tmin→Tdew assumption) produced large positive bias and large RMSE, especially at humid/mountainous sites (e.g., Caparaó) where it performed worst (RMSE up to 2.08 mm day⁻¹); HS overestimated ET0 in humid sites and underestimated in dry sites (systematic climate-dependent bias); HC regionalizations fitted poorly when regional climate heterogeneity existed (lower r² than in homogeneous regions such as southern Spain). Linear regression sometimes underestimates at particular stations (worst-case MAE up to 0.78 mm day⁻¹ at Presidente Kennedy).
extracted_data.unphysical_dewpoint_extremes: Not reported — the paper does not mention occurrences of unphysical dew-point extremes (e.g., Td exceeding plausible maxima) or RH>100% resulting from Tmin→Tdew substitution; no explicit clipping or physical implausibility diagnostics are described.
extracted_data.mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias: Not discussed — the study does not describe mechanisms for late dry-season humidity or Tmin–Td decoupling specific to Amazon/tropical lowlands (no discussion of biomass burning, advection, or convective regime shifts).
extracted_data.constraints_and_physical_plausibility_ch: None reported — the paper does not describe post-processing constraints (e.g., enforcing T_dew ≤ Tmin, RH bounds) or energy-balance consistency checks applied to derived vapor pressures or ET0 outputs.
extracted_data.data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues: Authors acknowledge potential sample/representativeness issues: only a five-year series (2009–2013) used, and regional HC methods suffer when climate heterogeneity exists; they included neighboring stations to reduce edge/frontier effects; they recommend longer time series and more locations for more robust local calibrations.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Key items: Table 1 (station list and climate), Fig. 2 (dispersion of HC vs Tmean/ΔT), Table 2 (Martí et al. model coefficients for HC), Eqns 4–5 (HC definitions), Eq. 6 and Eq. 12 (linear regression ET0 calibration: ET0 = 1.08 ET0_HS - 0.81), Fig. 3 (scatterplots of ET0 estimates vs PM), Table 3 (general performance metrics), Table 4 (site-level best/worst performance), Fig. 4 (effect of linear correction on ET0 scatter).

extracted_data.name_full: Penman-Monteith FAO-56 method applied with limited climatological data (PML) using Tmin to estimate dew-point/actual vapour pressure
extracted_data.brief_description: Implementation of FAO-56 guidance when RH, wind or radiation are missing: assume dew point temperature approximately equals daily minimum temperature to compute actual vapour pressure via Tetens' equation, assume wind speed = 2 m s⁻¹ if missing, and estimate radiation with the Hargreaves Rs proxy (k_Rs).
extracted_data.citation_title: Crop Evapotranspiration: guidelines for computing crop water requirements (FAO - Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56)
extracted_data.study_region: Applied and evaluated across 17 INMET stations in Espírito Santo and neighboring sites (2009–2013).
extracted_data.climate_zone_context: Tested across mixed climates (Aw, Am, Cfa/Cfb/Cwa/Cwb); worst performance occurred in humid/mountainous locations (Caparaó, Cwb).
extracted_data.target_variable_definition: Used Tmin as proxy for dew point T_po, then used Tetens' equation to compute actual vapour pressure e_a for use in Penman-Monteith ET0 calculation.
extracted_data.predictors_used: Tmin (for Tdew/e_a), Tmax/Tmin (for Hargreaves Rs), assumed wind speed 2 m s⁻¹, extraterrestrial radiation R_a and k_Rs coefficients (0.16 interior, 0.19 coastal).
extracted_data.fao56_assumption_details: Explicit implementation: assume T_dew ≈ Tmin at sunrise (near-saturated conditions), compute e_a from Tmin via Tetens; assume wind speed = 2 m s⁻¹ when missing; use Hargreaves Rs with k_Rs values 0.16–0.19 to estimate solar radiation.
extracted_data.model_family: Penman-Monteith physically based ET0 formula using substituted/estimated inputs (empirical proxy for missing vars).
extracted_data.localization_strategy: FAO-56 standard constants used (global defaults k_Rs, wind speed), no local tuning of Tmin→Tdew approximation beyond testing across stations.
extracted_data.seasonality_handling: None specific — PML applied daily using daily Tmin and Tmax; no seasonal correction to Tmin→Tdew assumption.
extracted_data.physical_mechanisms_for_skill: Underlying FAO-56 rationale: at near-sunrise temperatures approach daily minimum and boundary layer may be close to saturation so Tmin approximates dew point. No further mechanistic validation is made in this paper; authors report empirical failure in humid/mountainous contexts.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling: Not discussed specifically for PML; global FAO defaults applied rather than localized pooling.
extracted_data.validation_data_sources: Reference for skill evaluation: full-data Penman-Monteith ET0 (PM) computed from station radiation, RH and wind series; PML estimates compared against this PM reference.
extracted_data.performance_metrics: PML aggregated performance vs PM: MAE = 1.46 mm day⁻¹, MBE = 1.43 mm day⁻¹ (large positive bias), RMSE = 1.63 mm day⁻¹, RRMSE = 0.44, r² = 0.73. Site-level worst: Caparaó RMSE = 2.08 mm day⁻¹ and MAE = 1.91 mm day⁻¹.
extracted_data.comparators_and_baselines: Compared to PM full-data (reference) and to other temperature-based alternatives (HS, HC-adjusted HS, linear regression correction); PML performed worst of the tested approaches in this region.
extracted_data.reported_failure_modes: Strong positive bias and large RMSE particularly at humid/mountainous sites (Caparaó). Authors conclude PML performed worst among tested methods in Espírito Santo.
extracted_data.constraints_and_physical_plausibility_ch: Standard FAO-56 assumptions applied; authors did not report additional plausibility clipping or checks specific to Tmin→Tdew substitution.
extracted_data.data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues: Authors note that regional heterogeneity and station climate differences can reduce the validity of global FAO defaults; PML's poor performance may be exacerbated by local climatic characteristics not represented by global assumptions.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Fig. 3b (scatter of PML ET0 vs PM), Table 3 (aggregated PML performance), Table 4 (site-level PML best/worst).

extracted_data.name_full: Hargreaves and Samani (1985) empirical ET0 equation
extracted_data.brief_description: Temperature-based empirical equation to estimate reference evapotranspiration ET0 requiring only Tmax, Tmin and extraterrestrial radiation (or R_a via calendar), using the square root of the diurnal temperature range as a radiation proxy.
extracted_data.study_region: Applied across the 17 stations in Espírito Santo (2009–2013) as the uncalibrated baseline temperature-only estimator.
extracted_data.climate_zone_context: HS performance assessed across mixed climates; authors report HS tends to overestimate ET0 in humid regions and underestimate in dry regions in line with other studies.
extracted_data.target_variable_definition: Estimand is ET0 (reference evapotranspiration); HS does not directly reconstruct dew point or vapor pressure but its inputs and calibration interact with humidity assumptions used in PM-limited variants.
extracted_data.predictors_used: Tmax, Tmin (Tmean), diurnal range ΔT; R_a (extraterrestrial radiation) used in original formula (or R_s estimated by substituting with Hargreaves Rs when needed).
extracted_data.fao56_assumption_details: HS is an alternate temperature-based ET0 estimator recommended by FAO as an option when data are limited; study uses the original HS formula and also implements HC adjustments to calibrate HS to PM reference.
extracted_data.model_family: Empirical deterministic formula with a multiplicative HC coefficient (0.0023 factor in standard form); calibration of HC via regression or regionalization yields modified HS variants.
extracted_data.localization_strategy: Authors test several localization/calibration strategies for HS: (1) per-station daily HC computed and averaged per station; (2) regional HC estimated via Vanderlinden-style regression on Tmean/ΔT; (3) regional HC via Martí-style multiple regression on Tmean, ΔT and geographic variables; (4) direct ET0 linear regression correction (ET0 = a + b ET0_HS) calibrated across stations.
extracted_data.seasonality_handling: No DOY-specific HS adjustments were applied in the study; HC values were averaged per station across the entire 5-year period and regressions used those means.
extracted_data.physical_mechanisms_for_skill: HS leverages diurnal temperature range as an empirical proxy for incoming solar radiation/clear-sky conditions and hence available energy for ET; regional adjustments to HC account for local humidity/cloudiness/altitude effects that modulate the ΔT–radiation–ET0 link.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling: Authors pooled all daily data for calibration; they note pooled/regional calibrations worked less well when the region is climatically heterogeneous.
extracted_data.validation_data_sources: PM (full-data) ET0 was used as the reference for assessing raw and calibrated HS; performance summarized in Table 3.
extracted_data.performance_metrics: Original HS aggregated performance vs PM: MAE=0.68 mm day⁻¹, MBE=0.47 (overestimation), RMSE=0.83 mm day⁻¹, RRMSE=0.22, r²=0.78. Site-level best (Linhares) MAE=0.48; worst (Caparaó) MAE=0.91 and MBE=0.87.
extracted_data.comparators_and_baselines: Compared against PM full-data (reference), PML, HC-adjusted HS (Vanderlinden and Martí), and linear regression-corrected HS; linear regression correction improved HS estimates by up to ~30%.
extracted_data.reported_failure_modes: HS tends to overestimate ET0 in humid/mountainous sites and perform better in drier climates (e.g., Linhares). Systematic bias accumulates annually (authors estimate ~172 mm yr⁻¹ from 0.47 mm day⁻¹ bias).
extracted_data.unphysical_dewpoint_extremes: Not applicable/Not reported — HS is an ET0 estimator and the paper does not report HS producing unphysical dew points.
extracted_data.constraints_and_physical_plausibility_ch: No additional physical clipping applied to HS outputs; calibration was purely statistical.
extracted_data.data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues: Authors note that limited 5-year dataset and climate heterogeneity across stations influence the robustness of HC regionalizations; recommend longer records.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Eq. 2–3 (HS equations), Fig. 3a (HS vs PM scatter), Table 3 (HS performance), Table 4 (site-level HS best/worst).

extracted_data.name_full: Vanderlinden et al. (2004) method to regionalize the Hargreaves coefficient HC
extracted_data.brief_description: Regionalization method that models HC as HC = k1 * (Tmean / ΔT) + k2, where station mean HC (computed from ET0_PM/ET0_HS) is regressed against the ratio Tmean/ΔT to derive regional coefficients.
extracted_data.study_region: Applied to Espírito Santo stations using station mean HC and mean Tmean/ΔT from 2009–2013.
extracted_data.climate_zone_context: Method performed less well in the climatically heterogeneous Espírito Santo (r² lower than Vanderlinden's Spain results), but method captures HC variation tied to mean temperature and diurnal amplitude.
extracted_data.target_variable_definition: Targets the HC coefficient used to scale HS; HC computed daily as HC = 0.0023 * (ET0_PM / ET0_HS) and averaged per station for regression fitting.
extracted_data.predictors_used: Station mean ratio Tmean/ΔT (Tmean divided by thermal amplitude) as sole predictor in the canonical Vanderlinden formulation; other approaches (Martí) extend predictors.
extracted_data.fao56_assumption_details: Not specifically FAO-56; method is a regionalization for HS coefficient, used in conjunction with HS which can serve as FAO alternative.
extracted_data.model_family: Simple linear regression (HC as linear function of Tmean/ΔT).
extracted_data.localization_strategy: Regional regression across stations using station means (i.e., create one regional HC model for the study region). Evaluation in this paper used same data as fit (authors followed Vanderlinden's approach).
extracted_data.seasonality_handling: HC computed as station mean (averaging across season/day); no DOY decomposition.
extracted_data.physical_mechanisms_for_skill: Rationale: Tmean/ΔT ratio summarizes climatic regime (e.g., lower ΔT or higher Tmean associated with more humid/cloudy conditions) that modulates the HC required to match HS to PM.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling: Not explicitly discussed; method essentially collapses seasonal/DOY variability into station mean HC, assuming station climatology captures the dominant signal.
extracted_data.validation_data_sources: HC derived from PM reference ET0 and HS ET0 (daily), then averaged per station; regional regression coefficients estimated and reported (Eq. 11: HC = 0.00004 * Tmean/ΔT + 0.00011 in this study).
extracted_data.performance_metrics: Vanderlinden approach aggregated: MAE = 0.77 mm day⁻¹, MBE = 0.17, RMSE = 1.00 mm day⁻¹, RRMSE = 0.27, r² = 0.54 (lower than in Vanderlinden's original Spain results where r²≈0.90).
extracted_data.comparators_and_baselines: Compared against original HS, Martí HC models, PML, and linear regression correction. Vanderlinden performed better than PML but worse than simple global linear regression correction in this region.
extracted_data.reported_failure_modes: Fit quality degraded in a heterogeneous climatic region; lower r² suggests the single predictor Tmean/ΔT insufficient to capture HC variability across the diverse climates in Espírito Santo.
extracted_data.constraints_and_physical_plausibility_ch: None reported beyond ordinary regression diagnostics; authors compared coefficient magnitudes with Vanderlinden's original study.
extracted_data.data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues: Authors note that Vanderlinden's stronger results in Spain likely stem from climate homogeneity there; in Espírito Santo heterogeneity and limited station sample degrade regression performance.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Fig. 2 (HC dispersion vs Tmean/ΔT), Eq. 11 (fitted Vanderlinden relation), Table 3 (performance comparison).

extracted_data.name_short: Martí et al. (2015) HC multiple regression
extracted_data.name_full: Martí et al. (2015) method for HC adjustment using temperature and geographic variables
extracted_data.brief_description: Multiple linear regression approach to estimate HC from available station descriptors (Tmean, ΔT, latitude, longitude, altitude) enabling a regional HC model that uses easily accessible geographic inputs.
extracted_data.study_region: Martí-style models were fit to station mean HC across the Espírito Santo network; several model variants (1–8) combining temperature and geographic predictors were tested.
extracted_data.climate_zone_context: Tested across the state's varied climates; inclusion of geographic coordinates provided little improvement in this heterogeneous region compared to temperature-only models.
extracted_data.target_variable_definition: Predict HC (Hargreaves coefficient) to scale HS ET0 to PM reference.
extracted_data.predictors_used: Tmean, ΔT (base); optional latitude (τ), longitude (φ), altitude (z) included in different model variants. Example Model 7 in this study: HC = 7.00e-4 + 3.46e-5 Tmean - 1.13e-4 ΔT - 3.91e-5 φ - 1.10e-7 z (units as in paper).
extracted_data.fao56_assumption_details: Not directly FAO-56; this is HC regionalization to improve HS (an FAO-recommended temperature-only alternative).
extracted_data.model_family: Multiple linear regression (station-mean HC regressed on station covariates).
extracted_data.localization_strategy: Regional across all stations; models produce a regional mapping from geography/temperature stats to HC enabling application at ungauged locations with known coordinates/altitude/temperature climatology.
extracted_data.seasonality_handling: HC derived from station mean HC aggregated over 5-year record; no DOY-specific calibration.
extracted_data.physical_mechanisms_for_skill: Motivation: geographic variables capture regional climatological influences (coastal vs interior, altitude, latitude/longitude gradients) on the Tmin–Tdew/radiation relationship and thus on HC.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling: Not explicitly discussed; station-mean approach assumes climatological station characteristics encapsulate seasonal effects sufficiently for HC estimation.
extracted_data.validation_data_sources: HC computed from PM reference ET0 and HS ET0; multiple linear regressions fit to station-mean HC values. Table 2 reports model coefficients and fit metrics (RRMSE ~0.046–0.048, r² ~0.53–0.56).
extracted_data.performance_metrics: Best Martí model in study (model 7) gave RRMSE=0.046, r²=0.56, MAE (HC) ~7e-5 (dimensionless). When propagated to ET0, Martí aggregate ET0 performance: MAE=0.81 mm day⁻¹, MBE=-0.18, RMSE=1.01, RRMSE=0.27, r²=0.54.
extracted_data.comparators_and_baselines: Compared to Vanderlinden HC, original HS and linear regression ET0 correction. Martí models performed similarly to Vanderlinden in this dataset and worse than the global linear regression correction.
extracted_data.reported_failure_modes: Geographic covariates provided little improvement over temperature-only model in Espírito Santo (unlike Martí's results in eastern Spain), attributed to climate heterogeneity and limited sample size.
extracted_data.constraints_and_physical_plausibility_ch: None reported beyond regression performance metrics.
extracted_data.data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues: Authors note models may be limited by only five years of data and by the heterogeneity across stations; Martí's superior results in Spain likely due to regional homogeneity which is lacking here.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Table 2 (Martí model coefficients and fit statistics), Table 3 (propagated ET0 performance), Table 4 (site-level best/worst where Martí model performed).

extracted_data.name_full: Global linear regression calibration of HS ET0 to PM ET0 (ET0 = a + b * ET0_HS)
extracted_data.brief_description: A simple linear regression of PM ET0 against HS ET0 fit on pooled daily data produced a multiplicative and additive correction (ET0 = 1.08 * ET0_HS - 0.81), which reduced bias and overall error relative to other tested calibrations.
extracted_data.study_region: Fitted using pooled daily data from the 16/17 stations in Espírito Santo region for 2009–2013; evaluated with leave-one-out cross-validation so each station's evaluation used coefficients fit without that station's data.
extracted_data.climate_zone_context: Applied across all climates in the region; produced overall best aggregated performance but station-level performance varied (best in Serra dos Aimorés, worst in Presidente Kennedy).
extracted_data.target_variable_definition: Corrects HS-derived ET0 to match PM reference ET0; does not directly estimate dew point or vapor pressure but empirically corrects HS output that depends on Tmin/Tmax.
extracted_data.fao56_assumption_details: Not an FAO procedure — this is a statistical post-hoc correction of HS using PM as reference. It implicitly adjusts for systematic biases including those due to Tmin→Tdew mis-specification in PML or HS radiation proxy errors.
extracted_data.model_family: Ordinary least squares linear regression; evaluated with leave-one-out cross-validation for station-level assessment.
extracted_data.localization_strategy: Global/regional single regression fitted across all stations but evaluated in a cross-validated (leave-one-out) manner to approximate out-of-sample performance.
extracted_data.seasonality_handling: None explicit — coefficients are constant year-round (no DOY stratification).
extracted_data.physical_mechanisms_for_skill: Statistical correction captures average systematic offsets in HS (e.g., due to humidity/radiation biases) across pooled conditions; authors note it changes slope and intercept without changing dispersion (so r² unchanged but bias removed).
extracted_data.interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling: Authors used pooled daily data to estimate a single correction; they argue this is easily applied and performed best among tested methods, but they also recommend future work with day/condition-specific calibrations (Zanetti et al. 2019) for further improvement.
extracted_data.validation_data_sources: PM ET0 with full data used as target; regression coefficients reported (ET0 = 1.08 ET0_HS - 0.81) with r² = 0.78 (p < 0.01). Leave-one-out cross-validation used for station-level evaluation.
extracted_data.performance_metrics: Linear regression aggregated performance: MAE = 0.53 mm day⁻¹, MBE ≈ 0.00, RMSE = 0.68 mm day⁻¹, RRMSE = 0.18, r² = 0.78. Improved MAE by up to ~30% relative to original HS.
extracted_data.comparators_and_baselines: Outperformed original HS, Vanderlinden HC and Martí HC adjustments, and PML in aggregated metrics for this region.
extracted_data.reported_failure_modes: Although best on average, linear regression underperformed at some individual sites where it produced underestimation (e.g., Presidente Kennedy had MAE 0.78 mm day⁻¹ and MBE -0.60). Authors caution that longer series and site-specific calibrations could further improve results.
extracted_data.constraints_and_physical_plausibility_ch: No explicit physical constraints applied to corrected ET0 (correction purely statistical).
extracted_data.data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues: Authors used leave-one-out cross-validation to mitigate overfitting to stations; still emphasize the benefit of longer records and more stations for robust calibration.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Eq. 12 (ET0 = 1.08 ET0_HS - 0.81), Fig. 3e and Fig. 4 (scatter before/after correction), Table 3 (aggregated performance), Table 4 (site-level best/worst).

extracted_data.name_full: Approximate regression quantiles (based on M-functionals with correction)
extracted_data.brief_description: A method that fits parametric diurnal regression curves using M-functionals (Huber M-function) and applies a variance-based shrinkage correction to produce approximate conditional p-quantile curves (p = 0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95) of weather variables as functions of time of day and month.
extracted_data.study_region: Automatic Weather Station, Macquarie University (Sydney, Australia); four years of local AWS data (1994–1997) recorded at 15-minute intervals. No broader geographic coordinates or elevation ranges are provided in the paper.
extracted_data.climate_zone_context: Not explicitly classified in the paper; only the AWS at Macquarie University is specified. The paper does not discuss humid tropical lowlands, Amazon, or dry-season transitions.
extracted_data.target_variable_definition: The paper models several weather components (global radiation, wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, soil temperature, soil heat flux). The method is applied to wet-bulb temperature and relative humidity among others; dew-point temperature (Td), actual vapor pressure, or specific humidity are not explicitly modeled or reconstructed in this paper.
extracted_data.predictors_used: Primary predictor is time of day (X) within a month; models are parametric functions of time (cosine functions for temperature, RH, wet-bulb; polynomial-type daytime functions for radiation; max(constant, cosine) for wind). Tmin is not used as a predictor for reconstructing dew point in this paper and FAO-56 assumptions are not discussed.
extracted_data.model_family: Parametric diurnal regression models combined with robust M-estimation (M-functionals). Specifically: cosine-based parametric models for 24-hour variables (Y = A*cos(pi*(X+B)/12) + C + eps), polynomial-type daylight models for radiation, and special max-constant/cosine form for wind; estimation via empirical M-function minimization with Huber M-function (s = 1). The approximate quantiles are produced by applying a correction factor (kappa) to regression M-functionals.
extracted_data.localization_strategy: Seasonal/monthly localization: models are fitted separately for each month (the paper refers to 'typical for a given month' and fits curves for each of 48 months in the 4-year record). No per-station-vs-gridcell strategy is discussed beyond using the single AWS station.
extracted_data.seasonality_handling: Monthly models (parametric diurnal curve fitted for each month). The method therefore accounts for seasonality by separate month-specific model fits; within-month diurnal variation is modeled explicitly by the parametric form.
extracted_data.day_of_year_window: Implicit monthly pooling (i.e., data pooled per calendar month across years). No explicit day-of-year window lengths like 30/45 days are reported and no alternative DOY-window experiments are described.
extracted_data.anomaly_definition: No anomaly definitions are provided; the method models absolute values conditional on time-of-day and month (no explicit detrending or anomaly-based predictors are used).
extracted_data.autoregressive_or_lagged_terms: None reported. The models do not include lagged dew point/humidity or autoregressive terms.
extracted_data.physical_mechanisms_for_skill: The paper gives general diurnal/phenomenological explanations (e.g., daily minimum typically occurs just before sunrise and maximum in mid-afternoon), and notes heteroscedasticity of weather variables and the effect of cloud/diurnal cycle on variance. It does not provide mechanistic discussion specific to Tmin→Td coupling, nocturnal boundary-layer moisture coupling, or moisture advection processes.
extracted_data.interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling: The paper uses month-based pooling; the implicit rationale is parsimony and capturing a 'typical' monthly diurnal pattern while using limited-parameter models. It also remarks that use of convex M-functions and the correction reduces variance of estimators, suggesting a trade-off between variance and bias, but it does not explicitly analyze DOY-window width choices or provide a formal statistical justification for monthly pooling vs narrower/wider windows.
extracted_data.validation_data_sources: Validation/illustration uses the same AWS station data (15-minute measurements aggregated or plotted on daily/monthly scales) from Macquarie University (1994–1997). No independent radiosonde, flux-tower, reanalysis, or satellite validation datasets are used or reported.
extracted_data.performance_metrics: No standard error metrics (RMSE/MAE/R2) are reported for dew point or humidity reconstruction. The paper reports qualitative/check metrics: designed so approximately 5% of observed values lie below the 5% curve and 5% above the 95% curve; the shrinkage correction parameter kappa is reported numerically in examples (e.g., kappa = 0.8325 for wind speed example). Variance estimator used: sigma^2 estimated as mean squared residuals from median fit. No seasonal/regime breakdown of numeric skill scores is provided.
extracted_data.comparators_and_baselines: Main methodological comparison is between uncorrected regression M-quantiles (regression M-functionals) and the corrected approximate regression quantiles (with shrinkage factor kappa). For wind speed the paper shows that uncorrected M-quantiles produce overly wide separation and do not leave ~5% of data below the 5% curve, whereas corrected approximate quantiles restore expected coverage. No comparison against FAO-56, Tmin-based methods, persistence, climatology, or reanalysis is performed.
extracted_data.reported_failure_modes: The main failure mode reported is that uncorrected regression M-functionals (i.e., without the variance shrinkage correction) can produce substantially inflated conditional-quantile spreads so that the nominal coverage is violated (example: wind speed where no observed points fall below the 5% M-quantile). Instrument censoring (anemometer records low wind speeds between 0 and 0.2 m/s as 0.2 m/s) is identified as a data/mechanism-specific complication that can distort quantile fits if not modeled explicitly. The paper cautions that not using the correction (17) 'may obtain results significantly departing from any sensible modelling of conditional quantiles.'
extracted_data.unphysical_dewpoint_extremes: No mentions. The paper does not report unphysical dew-point values, RH>100% issues, or extremely high dew points in humid tropical lowlands; dew point estimation from Tmin and FAO-56-style failures are not discussed.
extracted_data.mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias: None reported. The paper does not discuss tropical dry-season transitions, biomass burning effects, moisture recycling, or related mechanisms.
extracted_data.constraints_and_physical_plausibility_ch: Two pragmatic checks are described: (1) the shrinkage correction kappa (kappa = sqrt(sigma^2/(sigma^2 + Var(G)))) is applied to regression M-functionals to reduce inflated spread and better match nominal quantile coverage; (2) for wind speed the model enforces a lower bound (an explicit max{...,0.2}) to mimic instrument censoring. There are no explicit general physical constraints for humidity/dew point (e.g., Td <= T or RH clipping) discussed in the paper.
extracted_data.data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues: The paper uses four years of high-frequency data but does not analyze station-network sparsity; it mentions that convex M-functions combined with the correction can reduce estimator variance and improve numerical stability, implying attention to small-sample variance issues, but does not provide formal sampling diagnostics. Monthly pooling across years is used to increase sample size per-month fit.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Figure 1 (global radiation first 72 hours, with regression quantiles), Figure 2 (global radiation for January with five regression quantile curves), Figure 3 (wet-bulb temperature with regression quantiles), Figure 4 (midday regression quantiles for global radiation over 48 months), Figure 5 (wind speed in August 1994: above shows uncorrected regression M-quantiles, below shows approximate regression quantiles after correction).

metadata.title: A 59-year (1948-2006) global near-surface meteorological data set for land surface models. Part I: Development of daily forcing and assessment of precipitation intensity
metadata.abstract: This paper describes the development and assessment of global 0.5° near-surface atmospheric data from 1948 to 2006 at daily (for precipitation, snowfall, and specific humidity) to 3-hourly (for temperature, shortwave radiation, and longwave radiation) time scales, which can be used to drive land surface models. Using newly available monthly precipitation and temperature data extending to recent years, the variables were created by statistical methods, the parameters of which were obtained from available daily to 3-hourly observations. The daily precipitation developed in this paper produces reasonable numbers of precipitation days and heavy precipitation days, different from previous longterm meteorological data sets based on reanalysis. Together with its relatively high spatial resolution (0.5°) and availability of recent years, the newly obtained data may be preferred to other forcing data sets in case of hydrological and climate change studies, in particular if the study results are sensitive to daily variations in atmospheric conditions.

| name_full | H08 specific-humidity / dew point estimation (Hirabayashi et al. 2008) |
| brief_description | In H08 daily specific humidity and downward longwave radiation are computed from an empirical equation model that estimates dew point (and related vapor quantities) as a function of daily precipitation, daily maximum and minimum temperature, and daily shortwave radiation; dew point coefficients were taken from an independent 1986–1995 atmospheric forcing data set to avoid unrealistic values in very dry grids. |
| citation_title | A 59-year (1948–2006) global near-surface meteorological data set for land surface models. Part I: Development of daily forcing and assessment of precipitation intensity |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region | Global land at 0.5° grid (1948–2006); regional replacements/augmentations over India (IMD) and East Asia (EA) where gauge products exist. |
| climate_zone_context | Global coverage including low-latitude (including humid tropical lowlands), mid-latitude and high-latitude regions; the paper highlights grids with very small annual precipitation (very dry) as problematic for the original dew-point model, and discusses gauge-sparse low-latitude regions where precipitation/humidity estimates are more uncertain. |
| target_variable_definition | Target variables: daily specific humidity and derived dew point temperature (Td) and downward longwave radiation. Td is estimated by an empirical, iterative equation model (originally from Hirabayashi et al. 2005) with coefficients derived from an independent 1986–1995 atmospheric forcing data set (Dirmeyer et al. 2006). |
| predictors_used | Predictors used in the empirical Td/q model: daily precipitation (disaggregated from monthly totals), daily maximum and minimum temperature (from stochastic weather generator output, scaled to monthly means), and daily shortwave radiation (SRB-scaled). Additional inputs used elsewhere for scaling: monthly mean temperature (Fan & van den Dool), monthly climatologies, and precipitation occurrence (Markov chain). Tmin is used (as one of Tmax/Tmin) but not the sole predictor. |
| fao56_assumption_details | None |
| model_family | Empirical equation model for Td/q (iterative solution until convergence in the prior formulation); stochastic weather generator (Richardson 1981) to create daily Tmax/Tmin and shortwave; gamma-distribution to disaggregate monthly precipitation into daily; first-order Markov chain for precipitation occurrence where needed. |
| localization_strategy | Coefficients for the dew-point empirical equations were obtained from a global 1986–1995 atmospheric forcing data set (Dirmeyer et al. 2006) rather than per-station calibration; stochastic-generator parameters were obtained from GTS 1986–1995 and stratified for wet vs dry days; regional substitution of gauge-based daily precipitation products was applied over India and East Asia where available. |
| seasonality_handling | Seasonality is handled via scaling to monthly climatologies: daily Tmax/Tmin are generated then scaled to monthly mean temperatures (Fan & van den Dool) and monthly mean temperature range (CRU/GTS); shortwave radiation scaled to monthly SRB; the dew-point coefficients themselves were derived from multi-year (1986–1995) forcing data (no explicit day-of-year model reported). |
| day_of_year_window | None |
| anomaly_definition | None |
| autoregressive_or_lagged_terms | None |
| physical_mechanisms_for_skill | Implicit rationale given by model choice: daily moisture (specific humidity / Td) is related to moisture supply (precipitation), near-surface temperature (Tmax/Tmin) and radiative forcing (shortwave); wet vs dry-day stratification for generator parameters recognizes differing thermodynamic/humidity regimes on wet and dry days. The paper does not explicitly derive boundary-layer mechanisms linking Tmin to Td. |
| interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling | None |
| validation_data_sources | Coefficients and some parameter estimation were taken from/obtained using: GTS daily observations (precipitation and Tmax/Tmin, 1986–1995), SRB shortwave radiation (1984–2004) and the Dirmeyer et al. (2006) atmospheric forcing data set (GSWP-2) used to obtain dew-point coefficients; however, no dedicated station-by-station validation of reconstructed daily Td/q is reported in this paper (validation focus is on precipitation statistics). |
| performance_metrics | No quantitative error metrics (RMSE/MAE/bias/correlation) for Td, specific humidity or vapor pressure are reported in this paper; validation/metrics are reported only for precipitation statistics (number of precipitation days, number of heavy precipitation days) and qualitative comparisons of precipitation spatial patterns. |
| comparators_and_baselines | For atmospheric variables generally the paper compares precipitation outputs to GTS, GPCP-1DD, ERA-40 and NCC; for dew point/specific humidity there are no explicit baseline comparisons (no FAO-56 Tmin-based baseline nor direct radiosonde/reanalysis Td comparisons reported). |
| reported_failure_modes | The original iterative empirical dew-point model (Hirabayashi et al. 2005) produced 'unrealistic values' on grids with very small annual precipitation; to avoid that, coefficients were replaced/obtained from the 1986–1995 Dirmeyer et al. (2006) forcing data. The paper also reports general data-sparsity related uncertainties in low latitudes due to few gauges and notes reanalysis-based precipitation products show unrealistic numbers of precipitation days and heavy-day frequency (this affects moisture estimates indirectly). |
| unphysical_dewpoint_extremes | The paper mentions 'unrealistic values' produced by the original dew-point estimator in very-low-precipitation grids but does not quantify specific unphysical Td magnitudes (no numerical examples of Td>physically-plausible thresholds or RH>100% are provided). |
| mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias | None |
| constraints_and_physical_plausibility_checks | The previous method involved iterative calculation until convergence; after identification of unrealistic outputs in dry grids, the authors replaced the coefficient set by coefficients derived from an independent 1986–1995 forcing data set to improve plausibility. No explicit other constraints (e.g., enforcing Td<=T or clipping RH to <=100%) are reported in the text. |
| data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues | The paper documents gauge sparsity issues: PREC/L gauge counts decline to <4000 in 2000s and are lower in low latitudes, GTS has fewer gauges (≈4000–6000) than PREC/L historically; these sampling issues motivated use of regional high-gauge products (IMD, EA) and using PREC/L monthly totals as a base. The authors note that limited gauge coverage in low latitudes leads to larger differences between products and increased uncertainty in moisture-related estimates. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Table I (data sources); Figure 1 (zonal means of precipitation days/heavy days); Figure 2 & 3 (spatial distribution of precipitation days and heavy precipitation days); Supplement 1 (process schematic); Supplement 2 & 3 (precipitation diagnostics). No figure directly shows Tmin–Td relationships or Td validation. |

metadata.title: An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1)
metadata.abstract: Abstract. Meteorological time series with 1 h time steps are required in many applications in geoscientific modelling. These hourly time series generally cover shorter periods of time compared to daily meteorological time series. We present an open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST). This software package is written in Python and comprises simple methods to temporally downscale (disaggregate) daily meteorological time series to hourly data. MELODIST is capable of disaggregating the most commonly used meteorological variables for geoscientific modelling including temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind speed, and shortwave radiation. In this way, disaggregation is performed independently for each variable considering a single site without spatial dependencies. The algorithms are validated against observed meteorological time series for five sites in different climates. Results indicate a good reconstruction of diurnal features at those sites. This makes the methodology interesting to users of models operating at hourly time steps, who want to apply their models for longer periods of time not covered by hourly observations.

content.title: Humidity disaggregation methods implemented in MELODIST (H1: Tdew=Tmin; H2: linear regression; H3: linear day-to-day variation + sine diurnal term; H4: min/max humidity redistribution)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | MELODIST humidity methods (H1–H4) |
| name_full | Humidity disaggregation methods implemented in MELODIST (H1: Tdew=Tmin; H2: linear regression; H3: linear day-to-day variation + sine diurnal term; H4: min/max humidity redistribution) |
| brief_description | The paper implements and validates four deterministic humidity disaggregation approaches that reconstruct hourly dew point temperature (Tdew) and derived actual vapour pressure/relative humidity from daily data: (H1) assume daily Tdew = daily Tmin (un-calibrated), (H2) calibrated linear relation Tdew_day = a*Tmin + b, (H3) diurnal Tdew(t) constructed from daily Tdew values with linear interpolation between days plus a sinusoidal diurnal perturbation (k_r dependent on monthly radiation), and (H4) interpolate between daily H_min and H_max using disaggregated hourly temperature. |
| citation_title | An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1) |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region | Five station-based sites used for calibration/validation: De Bilt, Netherlands (elevation 2 m); Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard (11 m); Obergurgl, Austria (1938 m); Rio de Janeiro – São Cristovão, Brazil (5 m); Tucson International Airport, USA (779 m). Split-sample calibration and validation periods are given per station (Table 1). |
| climate_zone_context | Multiple climates tested: mid-latitude maritime (De Bilt), Arctic polar / high-latitude (Ny-Ålesund), alpine (Obergurgl), humid tropical lowland / urban (Rio de Janeiro), subtropical desert / semi-arid (Tucson). Hydroclimate descriptors vary by site (annual precipitation shown in Fig.2); the methods are assessed across differing humidity regimes and seasonality. |
| target_variable_definition | Primary target: dew point temperature (Tdew) reconstructed at hourly resolution; actual vapour pressure ea computed as ea = es(Tdew) using the Magnus formula (Alduchov & Eskridge 1997); relative humidity RH computed as RH = 100 * ea / es(T) where T is the disaggregated hourly air temperature. The paper reconstructs Tdew first (H1–H3) or RH directly via min/max RH (H4). |
| predictors_used | Main predictor: daily minimum temperature (Tmin) used in H1 and as basis for H2/H3; other inputs: daily Tmax (for temperature disaggregation feeding RH), disaggregated hourly temperature (from T1) used to compute RH from Tdew, daily Hmin and Hmax for H4 when available; site-specific radiation/monthly mean radiation used in H3 (k_r set by monthly average radiation >100 W m^-2), sunshine/radiation used elsewhere for temperature/radiation disaggregation but not directly for H1/H2; methods otherwise rely on station-level observed daily values and locally calibrated parameters where applicable. |
| fao56_assumption_details | H1 implements the common simple assumption Tdew_day = Tmin (cited to Bregaglio et al., 2010 and Waichler & Wigmosta, 2003), which corresponds to the FAO-56 style heuristic often used in practice: using daily Tmin as a surrogate for daily dew point. The paper treats H1 as an uncalibrated baseline and notes that it is simple and sometimes acceptable but less reliable when only one daily humidity value is available, in polar/night conditions, or when local microclimate features decouple Tmin and Tdew. No FAO-56 document is directly cited; the paper frames H1 as the straightforward Tmin→Tdew assumption. |
| model_family | Deterministic simple models and local empirical calibration: (H1) deterministic identity Tdew=Tmin; (H2) ordinary linear regression Tdew_day = a*Tmin + b calibrated per site; (H3) deterministic day-to-day linear interpolation combined with an added sinusoidal diurnal perturbation (parameters from Debele et al., 2007); (H4) deterministic linear interpolation between daily Hmin/Hmax using disaggregated hourly temperature; no machine-learning, no AR models for humidity in this paper. |
| localization_strategy | Per-station/local calibration: H2 and H3 require calibration using hourly observations at the same site; many parameters are tuned per station (split-sample test used). Temperature disaggregation allows monthly/empirical shifts (T1c) determined from local hourly statistics. No regional/global pooled calibration strategy is applied in the humidity methods beyond using site-specific statistics and monthly radiation averages. |
| seasonality_handling | Seasonality addressed via simple local rules: H3 assumes mean daily Tdew occurs around sunrise and uses linear interpolation between consecutive daily Tdew values plus a sinusoidal diurnal term; the sinusoid parameter k_r is chosen by season-like criterion (k_r = 6 when average monthly radiation > 100 W m^-2, otherwise k_r = 12). Temperature disaggregation (T1) has an option (T1c) to apply empirical monthly shifts of Tmax timing; otherwise seasonality is implicitly handled by daily inputs and (for H3) the day-to-day linear interpolation. No advanced harmonic decomposition or DOY splines are implemented for humidity beyond these rules. |
| day_of_year_window | No explicit day-of-year smoothing/window lengths are specified for humidity models. The paper mentions monthly choices (T1c monthly empirical shifts; H3 uses monthly-average radiation for k_r), but does not implement explicit DOY pooling windows (e.g., 30- or 45-day moving windows) for Td–Tmin relationships. |
| anomaly_definition | The paper does not define or use anomaly-based predictors for dew point (no explicit Td' = Td - climatology(DOY) or similar anomaly modelling is reported). |
| autoregressive_or_lagged_terms | No autoregressive or lagged dew point/humidity predictors are used in the humidity methods described (H1–H4). H3 uses a day-to-day linear interpolation (so it links day d and day d+1) but not explicit AR(p) with estimated coefficients beyond that linear interpolation. |
| physical_mechanisms_for_skill | Mechanistic rationales provided in the paper: (1) nocturnal boundary-layer cooling and near-surface moisture coupling produce maximum RH / near-maximum Tdew around sunrise so daily Tmin is often a good proxy for daily dew point; (2) diurnal radiative forcing drives the temperature cycle, and temperature disaggregation assumes diurnal temperature follows incoming shortwave radiation (with phase shifts) which then controls RH when Tdew is fixed; (3) cloud cover and synoptic fronts modulate the timing/amplitude of Tmin and thus reduce the Tmin–Tdew coupling; (4) local microclimate effects (mountain-valley flows, land-sea breezes, cold-air drainage) influence diurnal cycles and can justify local calibration; (5) H3 explicitly assumes mean daily Tdew occurs near sunrise and adds a sinusoidal component to reflect sub-daily variability. |
| interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling | The paper does not explicitly advocate wide day-of-year pooling; it does highlight sampling limitations (limited hourly records) and station heterogeneity as reasons to favour parsimonious, locally calibrated models. It suggests monthly calibration/parameter estimation where data permit, and implies that broader pooling might be used when station sample size is small or when transferring parameters, but there is no formal discussion of a bias–variance tradeoff with DOY window widths. |
| validation_data_sources | Validation used station hourly observations (aggregated to daily for inputs and compared back to hourly observations) at the five AWS sites listed in Table 1: De Bilt (KNMI), Ny-Ålesund (AWI), Obergurgl (project data), Rio de Janeiro – São Cristovão (Alerta Rio), and Tucson International Airport (NOAA/NREL). Split-sample testing (separate calibration and validation periods) was applied. The Magnus formula (Alduchov & Eskridge, 1997) is used to compute saturation vapour pressure and invert between RH, T and Tdew. |
| performance_metrics | For humidity the paper reports hourly-validation statistics for the H3 method (Table 4) across stations: mean observed RH and mean disaggregated RH (percent), observed and simulated standard deviations (%), RMSE (%), Pearson correlation r, and Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE). Key numbers for H3 (validation): De Bilt: mean obs 81.82%, sim 81.63%, std_obs 15.12, std_sim 15.48, RMSE 12.67%, r=0.66, NSE=0.30. Ny-Ålesund: mean obs 74.96%, sim 74.82%, std_obs 12.61, std_sim 12.30, RMSE 17.41%, r=0.02, NSE=-0.91 (very poor). Obergurgl: mean obs 70.83%, sim 66.42%, RMSE 16.43%, r=0.51, NSE=0.14. Rio de Janeiro: mean obs 70.95%, sim 67.45%, RMSE 10.39%, r=0.72, NSE=0.46. Tucson: mean obs 35.31%, sim 33.31%, RMSE 18.52%, r=0.55, NSE=0.29. The paper emphasizes RMSE of order 10–20 % RH for the H3 method depending on site. |
| comparators_and_baselines | The paper compares H1 (Tdew=Tmin baseline), H2 (site-calibrated linear relation), H3 (diurnal/day-to-day interpolation + sinusoid) and H4 (use of daily Hmin/Hmax). H4 is reported as the best option when daily Hmin/Hmax are available (cited to Waichler & Wigmosta 2003). H3 is evaluated in Table 4 and shows variable performance by site; H1 is presented as a simple baseline and H2 as a calibrated improvement when hourly training data exist. No complex machine-learning baselines or reanalysis baselines are used for dew point in this study. |
| reported_failure_modes | Reported limitations/failure modes include: (1) very poor performance at Ny-Ålesund for H3 (RMSE 17.41%, r≈0, NSE negative), indicating the method fails in polar conditions / when radiation-driven diurnal cycles are weak or absent (polar night effects); (2) humidity disaggregation is generally less reliable when only one daily humidity-related value is available (i.e., H1–H3) because daily min/max humidity are not preserved; (3) fixed timing assumptions (for Tmin/Tmax) overestimate diurnal amplitude in some cases and fail during frontal passages or atypical synoptic conditions; (4) methods do not guarantee physical consistency across variables (no joint physical model), which can limit use for physics-based models; (5) dependency on quality and homogeneity of station records—changes in instrumentation or microclimate can degrade calibration transferability. |
| unphysical_dewpoint_extremes | The paper does not report occurrences of unphysical dew-point extremes (e.g., Td > Tmax, RH>100% or extremely high Td in humid tropics) nor does it document cases of Td overshoot in humid tropical lowlands or during dry-season transitions. No explicit instances of supersaturation or Td exceeding physically plausible thresholds are described. |
| mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias | The paper does not discuss mechanisms for late dry-season biases in tropical lowlands or Amazon-like regimes (e.g., biomass burning, moisture recycling, convective regime shifts) and does not report specific dry-season Td decoupling phenomena; it only notes that cascade/statistics-based methods and changing climate may require circulation-based parameterisations in future work. |
| constraints_and_physical_plausibility_checks | No explicit post-processing clipping or additional constraint routines are described for preventing unphysical values. Physical consistency is implicitly enforced by computing RH via e_s(Tdew)/e_s(T) (Magnus formula), but the paper does not state explicit checks to force Tdew <= T or to clip RH to [0,100%]. H4 uses observed daily Hmin/Hmax which inherently respects bounds if the input data are consistent. |
| data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues | The paper explicitly highlights limited availability of long hourly records (hourly AWS records are recent and sparse), potential inhomogeneities in long records (instrumentation, microclimate, processing changes), and the limited length of hourly training data as constraints on parameter estimation and transferability. These sampling issues motivate parsimonious models and local per-station calibration and caution against blind transfer of parameters across climates. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Key locations in the paper: Table 2 (overview of disaggregation methods, listing H1–H4), Table 4 (performance metrics for humidity disaggregation using H3 across sites), Fig. 4 (example application of different humidity disaggregation models for Obergurgl with RMSEs), Fig. 10 (long-term averaged diurnal cycles of observed and disaggregated relative humidity for H3 across all stations), Table 1 (station list and calibration/validation periods), and the methods section 3.3 (explicit formulas for H1–H4 and Magnus formula in Eq. 4 and inversion in Eq. 6). |

metadata.title: Future humidity trends over the western United States in the CMIP5 global climate models and variable infiltration capacity hydrological modeling system
metadata.abstract: Abstract. Global climate models predict relative humidity (RH) in the western US will decrease at a rate of about 0.1–0.6 percentage points per decade, albeit with seasonal differences (most drying in spring and summer), geographical variability (greater declines in the interior), stronger reductions for greater anthropogenic radiative forcing, and notable spread among the models. Although atmospheric moisture content increases, this is more than compensated for by higher air temperatures, leading to declining RH. Fine-scale hydrological simulations driven by the global model results should reproduce these trends. It is shown that the MT-CLIM meteorological algorithms used by the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) hydrological model, when driven by daily Tmin, Tmax, and precipitation (a configuration used in numerous published studies), do not preserve the original global model's humidity trends. Trends are biased positive in the interior western US, so that strong RH decreases are changed to weak decreases, and weak decreases are changed to increases. This happens because the MT-CLIM algorithms VIC incorporates infer an overly large positive trend in atmospheric moisture content in this region, likely due to an underestimate of the effect of increasing aridity on RH. The result could downplay the effects of decreasing RH on plants and wildfire. RH trends along the coast have a weak negative bias due to neglect of the ocean's moderating influence. A numerical experiment where the values of Tdew are altered to compensate for the RH error suggests that eliminating the atmospheric moisture bias could, in and of itself, decrease runoff up to 14% in high-altitude regions east of the Sierra Nevada and Cascades, and reduce estimated Colorado River runoff at Lees Ferry up to 4% by the end of the century. It could also increase the probability of large fires in the northern and central US Rocky Mountains by 13 to 60%.

metadata.title: Satellite-based near-real-time global daily terrestrial evapotranspiration estimates
metadata.abstract: Abstract. Accurate and timely global evapotranspiration (ET) data are crucial for agriculture, water resource management, and drought forecasting. Although numerous satellite-based ET products are available, few offer near-real-time data. For instance, products like NASA's ECOsystem Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment mounted on the International Space Station (ECOSTRESS) and MOD16 face challenges such as uneven coverage and delays exceeding 1 week in data availability. In this study, we refined the Variation of the Standard Evapotranspiration Algorithm (VISEA) by fully integrating satellite-based data, e.g., European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ERA5-Land shortwave radiation (which includes satellite remote sensing data within its assimilation system) and MODIS land surface data (which include surface reflectance, temperature and/or emissivity, land cover, vegetation indices, and albedo as inputs). This enables VISEA to provide near-real-time global daily ET estimates with a maximum delay of 1 week at a resolution of 0.05°. Its accuracy was assessed globally using observation data from 149 flux towers across 12 land cover types and comparing them with five other satellite-based ET products and Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) data. The results indicate that VISEA provides accurate ET estimates that are comparable to existing products, achieving a mean correlation coefficient (R) of about 0.6 and an RMSE of 1.4 mm d−1. Furthermore, we demonstrated VISEA's utility in drought monitoring during a drought event in the Yangtze River basin in 2022 in which ET changes correlated with precipitation. The near-real-time capability of VISEA is, thus, especially valuable in meteorological and hydrological applications for coordinating drought relief efforts. The VISEA ET dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.11888/Terre.tpdc.300782 (Huang, 2023a).

content.title: Vegetation Index–Land Surface Temperature (VI–Ts) method as implemented in the VISEA algorithm for estimating near-surface air temperature (Ta)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | VI–Ts / VISEA Ta estimation |
| name_full | Vegetation Index–Land Surface Temperature (VI–Ts) method as implemented in the VISEA algorithm for estimating near-surface air temperature (Ta) |
| brief_description | An empirical approach that uses the negative relationship between vegetation index (VI) and satellite land-surface temperature (Ts) in a local spatial neighborhood (5×5 grid cells) to estimate instantaneous air temperature during daytime (lowest Ts at high VI taken as Ta), complemented by nighttime LST for nocturnal Ta, extended to daily Ta by sine–cosine diurnal fitting; used inside the VISEA Penman–Monteith based ET framework. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region | Global application; VISEA is applied globally at 0.05° resolution and validated against 149 FLUXNET towers distributed worldwide (sites cover 12 IGBP land cover types). |
| climate_zone_context | All climate regimes globally are considered; paper highlights issues in temperate cold regions (dense/deciduous forests, DNF/MF), savannas (SAV) with pronounced wet/dry season transitions, humid tropical lowlands (Amazon, Congo, SE Asia) and high-latitude/cold regions (>60°N) where VI–Ts or radiation inputs have issues. |
| target_variable_definition | Daily near-surface air temperature (Ta) is estimated from satellite land-surface temperature (Ts) and VI; dew-point temperature (Td), vapor pressure, specific humidity, or relative humidity are not directly reconstructed by VISEA in this paper (Ta is used to compute radiation/emissivity and ET). |
| predictors_used | MODIS land-surface temperature/emissivity (MOD11C1), MODIS vegetation index (MOD13C1) and albedo (MCD43C3), ERA5-Land hourly downward shortwave radiation (ERA5_Rd) (interpolated to 0.05°), daytime and nighttime MODIS LST snapshots, 5×5 spatial neighborhood of VI–Ts for triangle method; no use of in-situ Tmin as a primary predictor for Ta in VISEA (Ta derived from Ts/VI), no explicit use of Tmin→Td conversions in VISEA. |
| fao56_assumption_details | FAO (1998) is cited but only for computing extraterrestrial radiation (Ra) used in the clearness index (Eq. 14). The FAO-56 assumption T_dew ≈ T_min (a common FAO-56 approach to estimate vapor pressure when humidity data are missing) is not applied or discussed as part of VISEA; no use of Tmin≈Tdew or simple Tmin-based humidity reconstruction is reported. |
| model_family | Hybrid physics-empirical: a Penman–Monteith based two-source ET model (VISEA) combined with empirical VI–Ts triangle method for Ta estimation; includes analytical decoupling-parameter transforms (based on Penman–Monteith / McNaughton–Jarvis) to convert instantaneous EF to daily EF. Not a pure statistical regression (no RF/NN), but uses empirical parameter estimation and physical formulae. |
| localization_strategy | Local spatial neighborhood: VI–Ts triangle method uses scatter of VI vs Ts in a 5×5 neighboring grid window to determine warm and cold edges and interpolate Ta per grid cell. No per-station regression calibration is applied; validation is per flux-tower site but model is globally applied with local 5×5 neighborhoods. Gap-filling of MODIS uses temporal neighbors (neighboring days) rather than station-specific calibration. |
| seasonality_handling | Seasonality handled implicitly by using daily MODIS observations and ERA5 inputs; diurnal cycle explicitly modelled by fitting sine–cosine curves to daytime (VI–Ts-derived) and nighttime LST-derived Ta to produce hourly profiles and 24 h averages; an explicit day-of-year pooling or per-DOY calibration is NOT reported for Ta estimation. |
| day_of_year_window | No explicit day-of-year smoothing/pooling window is described for Ta estimation; the VI–Ts method uses spatial 5×5 windows (not DOY windows). Temporal gap-filling of MODIS uses neighboring days but window length is not specified numerically beyond 'neighboring days'. |
| anomaly_definition | No explicit definition or use of anomalies (e.g., Ta' = Ta - climatology(DOY)) for Ta or humidity reconstruction is reported. |
| autoregressive_or_lagged_terms | No autoregressive (AR) or lagged Td/Ta predictors are reported. Temporal extension uses deterministic sine–cosine diurnal fitting between daytime and nighttime estimates rather than AR models or lagged persistence terms. |
| physical_mechanisms_for_skill | Mechanisms cited: (1) Negative empirical relationship between VI and Ts: vegetated surfaces remain cooler (cold edge) and bare/hot surfaces are warmer (warm edge), enabling interpolation of Ts→Ta; (2) assumption that the minimum LST within a local VI–Ts triangle corresponds to near-surface air temperature (Ta) in fully vegetated pixels; (3) nighttime LST approximates nocturnal air temperature; (4) coupling of radiative forcing (ERA5 shortwave) with land-surface energy balance allows translating EF into daily ET. These provide a physical rationale for why satellite Ts and VI contain information about Ta and thus about energy terms controlling ET. |
| interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling | Not applicable — the algorithm favors spatial pooling (5×5 VI–Ts window) rather than wide day-of-year pooling; paper does not advocate wide DOY pooling and instead notes that seasonal changes can break the VI–Ts relationship in some regions. |
| validation_data_sources | Ground-truth: FLUXNET2015 eddy-covariance measurements (149 selected towers, 2001–2015 subset for many analyses) used to validate ET, Ta, Rn and incoming shortwave. Additional radiative validation using CERES and ERA5 comparisons; evaluation statistics per IGBP land cover type (Figures 3–6). Data quality: selection criteria excluded sites with zero ERA5_Rd and ensured flux tower is over land per MOD12C1; standard FLUXNET QC procedures implied (Pastorello et al., 2020). |
| performance_metrics | Ta: VISEA_Ta vs observations: NSE range −0.22 to 0.82 across land covers, R range 0.44–0.97, RMSE range ≈5.7–11.2 K depending on land cover (examples: OSH NSE=0.82 R=0.93 RMSE=6.6 K; MF worst NSE=−0.22 R=0.44 RMSE=11.2 K). Shortwave radiation (ERA5_Rd vs obs): mean NSE=0.84, mean R=0.92, mean RMSE=38.3 W m−2 (savanna SAV notably poor: NSE=0.29 R=0.59 RMSE=63.2 W m−2). Net radiation (VISEA_Rn vs obs): mean NSE=0.49 mean R=0.74 mean RMSE=43.3 W m−2. ET (VISEA_ET vs flux towers): mean R≈0.56 (per flux towers), mean RMSE ≈1.4 mm d−1, mean NSE across sites ≈ −0.08 for daily comparisons but monthly comparisons in Taylor diagrams show mean CC 0.69 and mean RMSE (monthly) 31.6 mm month−1 (Table 3); abstract reports mean R≈0.6 and RMSE≈1.4 mm d−1. |
| comparators_and_baselines | Compared against five satellite/reanalysis ET products: GLEAM, FLUXCOM, AVHRR, MOD16, and PML; radiation inputs compared ERA5 vs CERES; baseline measures include flux-tower observations and GPCC precipitation for hydrological context. Sensitivity tests show VISEA performs better with CERES radiation (higher R and lower RMSE) than with ERA5 radiation. |
| reported_failure_modes | Known failure modes described: (1) VI–Ts method breakdown in dense/seasonal forests (DNF, MF) and cold regions where VI–Ts correlation can be positive (leads to systematic Ta errors); (2) savannas (SAV) exhibit poor ERA5 shortwave radiation skill and VI–Ts problems during dry/wet season transitions (VI→0 in dry season producing homogeneously high Ts; wet season both VI and Ts high with limited variance), causing large biases in Ta, Rn, and ET; (3) net radiation is systematically underestimated (~30% underestimation) in many land-cover types, possibly due to footprint vs grid-scale albedo differences and biases in inputs; (4) VISEA tends to underestimate ET in cold/high-latitude regions due to omission of frozen-surface evaporation and radiation/temperature input uncertainties; (5) VISEA may overestimate ET in tropical energy-limited regions because soil moisture/water availability is not explicitly included. |
| unphysical_dewpoint_extremes | No mentions: the paper does not report reconstructing dew-point temperature (Td) or any occurrences of unphysical high dew points, RH>100% errors, or supersaturation artifacts. No explicit reports of unphysical dew-point extremes in humid tropical lowlands or other regions are present. |
| mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias | For savannas and seasonal transition regions, mechanisms described include: dominance of bare soil in dry season (VI→0) producing uniformly high Ts and break-down of VI–Ts triangle; wet-season limited spatial variance in VI/Ts undermining interpolation; biases in ERA5_Rd due to land-use change, aerosols, and cloud/rainy-season misrepresentation. The paper mentions aerosols and cloudiness affecting radiation simulation in savannas and that such factors contribute to late dry-season bias and Ta/Rn/ET decoupling, but does not elaborate on dew-point specific processes (e.g., moisture advection or biomass burning effect on Tmin→Td coupling). |
| constraints_and_physical_plausibility_checks | Model constraints/choices: water surfaces are handled separately using Priestley–Taylor equation; decoupling factor Ω used to convert instantaneous EF to daily EF based on physical Penman–Monteith/McNaughton–Jarvis relations; no explicit clipping of humidity/dew point values or RH checks are reported because VISEA does not reconstruct Td directly. Emissivity and atmospheric emissivity calculated following Brutsaert (1975) and Wang & Dickinson (2013) procedures (Appendix D) to improve physical plausibility of radiation terms. |
| data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues | Noted issues: scale mismatch between flux-tower footprints (100–200 m) and 0.05° (~25 km2) grid cells causes representativeness errors; VI–Ts requires sufficient spatial variance in VI and Ts within 5×5 window — lack of variance in deserts, dense forests, or homogeneous regions undermines Ta estimation; station sparsity and mismatch in vegetation fraction between tower footprint and grid-average can lead to systematic Rn/ET biases; gap filling of MODIS (cloud gaps ~1/3 of period) uses neighboring days and was evaluated (cloud vs clear days performance shown), but temporal sampling gaps are a potential source of error. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Figures 3 (ERA5_Rd vs observations by land cover), 4 (VISEA_Ta vs observations by land cover), 5 (VISEA_Rn vs observations), 6 (VISEA_ET vs flux-tower ET), 7 (Taylor diagrams comparing monthly ET products), 8 (spatial distribution and zonal means), 9 (Yangtze River basin drought case study); Tables 1 (input datasets), 2 (comparison ET products), 3 (statistical metrics for ET products); Appendices A–D (detailed parameter/resistance/emissivity calculations). |
