metadata.title: Application of different calibration methods for the Hargreaves-Samani model in Southeast Brazil
metadata.abstract: The evapotranspiration is an important variable in the hydrological cycle and one of the main components of water balance in the soil. The use of simplified equations is a potential alternative to estimate reference evapotranspiration (ET 0 ) when there is limited meteorological data. The objective of this study was to test different methods to estimate ET 0 using the Hargreaves-Samani equation (HS) under different meteorological conditions. ET 0 was calibrated with HS, adjusting the HS coefficient (HC), using different methods. Adjustment by linear regression was also performed. ET 0 was also estimated using the original HS and Penman-Monteith FAO-56 methods with limited climatic data (PML). The performance of the methods (mean absolute error, mm day -1 ) to estimate evapotranspiration, based on Penman-Monteith, were: PML (1.46); HS (0.68); Vanderlinden et al. (2004) (0.81); Marti et al. (2015) (0.77); and linear regression (0.53). The PML method presented the worst performance. Adjustment by linear regression presented a better performance than the adjustments of HC, improving the ET 0 estimates by up to 30%, and it is considered the most recommendable of the methods tested.

content.title: Application of different calibration methods for the Hargreaves-Samani model in Southeast Brazil

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | This study (Espírito Santo 2009-2013) |
| name_full | Application of different calibration methods for the Hargreaves-Samani model in Southeast Brazil |
| brief_description | Case study comparing several approaches to estimate reference evapotranspiration (ET0) using temperature-based methods and Penman-Monteith (PM) as reference, including evaluation of the FAO-56 limited-data assumption that dew point ≈ Tmin, regional HC parameterizations, and a global linear regression correction. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region | State of Espírito Santo, southeast Brazil (approx. lat 17°52'–21°19' S, lon 39°38'–41°50' W); 17 weather stations (9 inside state + 8 neighboring), elevations ~9–976 m; daily observations 2009–2013. |
| climate_zone_context | Mixed climates within the state: Aw (tropical savanna with dry season), Am (monsoon), Cfa/Cfb/Cwa/Cwb (temperate/humid variants) per Köppen; mean annual precipitation 1,000–1,600 mm and mean annual temperature 18–24 °C; study explicitly contrasts drier (e.g., Linhares, Aw) vs humid/mountainous sites (e.g., Caparaó, Cwb). |
| target_variable_definition | Primary modeled quantity in study is reference evapotranspiration ET0. For FAO-56 limited-data (PML) application the actual vapour pressure e_a is estimated by computing dew point temperature T_dew from Tmin (i.e., assuming T_dew ≈ Tmin) using Tetens' equation; study does not directly reconstruct specific humidity or VPD but the e_a/T_dew assumption is central to PML. |
| predictors_used | Predictors used across methods: daily Tmin (primary predictor for dew point/e_a in PML), Tmax, Tmean, diurnal temperature range ΔT (Tmax–Tmin), extraterrestrial radiation R_a (and Hargreaves Rs proxy), station latitude/longitude/altitude for regional HC models; when PM used as reference it used full meteorological inputs (radiation, RH, wind) available from INMET. For PML, wind speed is substituted with a constant 2 m s⁻¹ and Rs estimated with Hargreaves temperature-based equation (kRs). |
| fao56_assumption_details | FAO-56 limited-data procedure implemented: assume dew point temperature T_po ≈ Tmin at sunrise so actual vapor pressure e_a computed from Tmin via Tetens' formula; assume wind speed = 2 m s⁻¹ if missing; estimate Rs with Hargreaves equation R_s = k_Rs R_a sqrt(Tmax - Tmin) with k_Rs = 0.16 (interior) or 0.19 (coastal) per FAO guidance. Study reports that applying these FAO-56 limited-data assumptions (PML) produced the worst ET0 performance (large positive bias) in this region. |
| model_family | Empirical temperature-based models and linear regressions: Hargreaves-Samani original empirical formula; HC (Hargreaves coefficient) regionalization via simple linear regression forms (Vanderlinden-style: HC = k1 * Tmean/ΔT + k2) and multiple linear regression (Martí-style) using Tmean, ΔT and geographic variables; global/simple linear calibration ET0 = a + b * ET0_HS (ordinary least squares). No machine learning (RF/NN) or AR time-series models were used in this study. |
| localization_strategy | Local and regional strategies tested: (a) per-station mean HC computed from daily HC then a regional regression across stations (Vanderlinden approach); (b) regional multiple linear regression of mean station HC on Tmean, ΔT and coordinates/altitude (Martí approach) to get regional HC; (c) global linear regression (ET0_PM vs ET0_HS) fit using all stations, with leave-one-out cross-validation applied when evaluating station performance to avoid bias. The HC adjustments are regional (fit across stations) while the linear ET0 correction was evaluated with cross-station validation. |
| seasonality_handling | No explicit day-of-year or monthly models were used; HC regressions were built from mean station HC values (averaged over the 5-year period), and the ET0 linear correction was fitted on daily data pooled across the full period (no DOY-specific coefficients). The study notes but does not implement per-day calibrated approaches (refers to Zanetti et al. 2019 as a promising per-condition calibration). |
| day_of_year_window | Not used — study did not apply explicit DOY-window smoothing or monthly bins; HC was averaged per station over the full record and regressions used those station means; linear regression calibration used daily pooled data (no DOY window). |
| anomaly_definition | None reported — anomalies (departure from climatology) were not defined or used in the tested methods. |
| autoregressive_or_lagged_terms | None — no lagged dew point/ea or autoregressive predictors were included in any tested method. |
| physical_mechanisms_for_skill | Mechanistic rationale reported/discussed: FAO-56 assumption relies on near-saturated conditions at sunrise so Tmin approximates dew point (Tdew≈Tmin); Hargreaves methods exploit diurnal temperature range as a proxy for radiation/clear-sky conditions (larger ΔT indicates more insolation and higher ET0); regional differences (humidity, cloudiness, coastal influence) change the Tmin–Tdew relationship and thereby HC, explaining why local/regional calibration improves skill; also climate homogeneity (as in southern Spain) yields better HC parameter fits than heterogeneous regions like Espírito Santo. |
| interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling | Implicit interpretation: study pooled daily data across seasons and stations to fit regional HC and global ET0 correction, noting that pooled/regional fits perform worse where climate heterogeneity is larger (they attribute Vanderlinden's stronger fit in Spain to climate homogeneity). The paper does not explicitly test or recommend wide DOY windows; instead it suggests that per-day/condition calibration might improve performance. |
| validation_data_sources | Ground truth: Penman-Monteith (FAO-56) ET0 computed using full INMET station data (where available) used as the reference. Input/validation stations: INMET network (17 stations total: 9 in ES + 8 neighboring), daily Tmax, Tmin, global solar radiation, relative humidity and wind speed for 2009–2013; days with data failures were discarded. Quality control: authors used previously-processed dataset from Xavier et al. (2015) and removed days with failures. |
| performance_metrics | Reported metrics: MAE, MBE (bias), RMSE, RRMSE (relative RMSE), and r² between estimated ET0 and PM reference. Key aggregated results (all stations combined): Hargreaves-Samani (original) MAE=0.68 mm day⁻¹, MBE=0.47, RMSE=0.83, RRMSE=0.22, r²=0.78; PML (FAO-56 limited-data) MAE=1.46, MBE=1.43, RMSE=1.63, RRMSE=0.44, r²=0.73; Martí et al. (HC regression) MAE=0.81, MBE=-0.18, RMSE=1.01, RRMSE=0.27, r²=0.54; Vanderlinden et al. (HC regression) MAE=0.77, MBE=0.17, RMSE=1.00, RRMSE=0.27, r²=0.54; Linear regression correction MAE=0.53, MBE≈0.00, RMSE=0.68, RRMSE=0.18, r²=0.78. Site-level best/worst per-method statistics are listed in Table 4. |
| comparators_and_baselines | Baselines compared: Penman-Monteith with full data (reference), Penman-Monteith limited-data (PML) using FAO-56 assumptions, Hargreaves-Samani original, HC-adjusted HS (Vanderlinden and Martí formulations), and a global linear regression correction. Quantitatively, PML performed worst (large bias MAE~1.46 mm day⁻¹), linear regression correction performed best (reduced MAE by up to ~30% vs original HS). |
| reported_failure_modes | Reported failure modes: PML (FAO-56 limited-data with Tmin→Tdew assumption) produced large positive bias and large RMSE, especially at humid/mountainous sites (e.g., Caparaó) where it performed worst (RMSE up to 2.08 mm day⁻¹); HS overestimated ET0 in humid sites and underestimated in dry sites (systematic climate-dependent bias); HC regionalizations fitted poorly when regional climate heterogeneity existed (lower r² than in homogeneous regions such as southern Spain). Linear regression sometimes underestimates at particular stations (worst-case MAE up to 0.78 mm day⁻¹ at Presidente Kennedy). |
| unphysical_dewpoint_extremes | Not reported — the paper does not mention occurrences of unphysical dew-point extremes (e.g., Td exceeding plausible maxima) or RH>100% resulting from Tmin→Tdew substitution; no explicit clipping or physical implausibility diagnostics are described. |
| mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias | Not discussed — the study does not describe mechanisms for late dry-season humidity or Tmin–Td decoupling specific to Amazon/tropical lowlands (no discussion of biomass burning, advection, or convective regime shifts). |
| constraints_and_physical_plausibility_checks | None reported — the paper does not describe post-processing constraints (e.g., enforcing T_dew ≤ Tmin, RH bounds) or energy-balance consistency checks applied to derived vapor pressures or ET0 outputs. |
| data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues | Authors acknowledge potential sample/representativeness issues: only a five-year series (2009–2013) used, and regional HC methods suffer when climate heterogeneity exists; they included neighboring stations to reduce edge/frontier effects; they recommend longer time series and more locations for more robust local calibrations. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Key items: Table 1 (station list and climate), Fig. 2 (dispersion of HC vs Tmean/ΔT), Table 2 (Martí et al. model coefficients for HC), Eqns 4–5 (HC definitions), Eq. 6 and Eq. 12 (linear regression ET0 calibration: ET0 = 1.08 ET0_HS - 0.81), Fig. 3 (scatterplots of ET0 estimates vs PM), Table 3 (general performance metrics), Table 4 (site-level best/worst performance), Fig. 4 (effect of linear correction on ET0 scatter). |

| brief_description | Temperature-based empirical equation to estimate reference evapotranspiration ET0 requiring only Tmax, Tmin and extraterrestrial radiation (or R_a via calendar), using the square root of the diurnal temperature range as a radiation proxy. |
| citation_title | Reference crop evapotranspiration from temperature. |
| mention_or_use | use |

| target_variable_definition | Estimand is ET0 (reference evapotranspiration); HS does not directly reconstruct dew point or vapor pressure but its inputs and calibration interact with humidity assumptions used in PM-limited variants. |

| seasonality_handling | No DOY-specific HS adjustments were applied in the study; HC values were averaged per station across the entire 5-year period and regressions used those means. |
| day_of_year_window | None. |
| anomaly_definition | None. |
| autoregressive_or_lagged_terms | None. |
| physical_mechanisms_for_skill | HS leverages diurnal temperature range as an empirical proxy for incoming solar radiation/clear-sky conditions and hence available energy for ET; regional adjustments to HC account for local humidity/cloudiness/altitude effects that modulate the ΔT–radiation–ET0 link. |
| interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling | Authors pooled all daily data for calibration; they note pooled/regional calibrations worked less well when the region is climatically heterogeneous. |
| validation_data_sources | PM (full-data) ET0 was used as the reference for assessing raw and calibrated HS; performance summarized in Table 3. |
| performance_metrics | Original HS aggregated performance vs PM: MAE=0.68 mm day⁻¹, MBE=0.47 (overestimation), RMSE=0.83 mm day⁻¹, RRMSE=0.22, r²=0.78. Site-level best (Linhares) MAE=0.48; worst (Caparaó) MAE=0.91 and MBE=0.87. |
| comparators_and_baselines | Compared against PM full-data (reference), PML, HC-adjusted HS (Vanderlinden and Martí), and linear regression-corrected HS; linear regression correction improved HS estimates by up to ~30%. |
| reported_failure_modes | HS tends to overestimate ET0 in humid/mountainous sites and perform better in drier climates (e.g., Linhares). Systematic bias accumulates annually (authors estimate ~172 mm yr⁻¹ from 0.47 mm day⁻¹ bias). |
| unphysical_dewpoint_extremes | Not applicable/Not reported — HS is an ET0 estimator and the paper does not report HS producing unphysical dew points. |
| mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias | Not discussed for HS specifically. |
| constraints_and_physical_plausibility_checks | No additional physical clipping applied to HS outputs; calibration was purely statistical. |
| data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues | Authors note that limited 5-year dataset and climate heterogeneity across stations influence the robustness of HC regionalizations; recommend longer records. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Eq. 2–3 (HS equations), Fig. 3a (HS vs PM scatter), Table 3 (HS performance), Table 4 (site-level HS best/worst). |

content.title: Vanderlinden et al. (2004) method to regionalize the Hargreaves coefficient HC

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Vanderlinden HC (2004) approach |
| name_full | Vanderlinden et al. (2004) method to regionalize the Hargreaves coefficient HC |
| brief_description | Regionalization method that models HC as HC = k1 * (Tmean / ΔT) + k2, where station mean HC (computed from ET0_PM/ET0_HS) is regressed against the ratio Tmean/ΔT to derive regional coefficients. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region | Applied to Espírito Santo stations using station mean HC and mean Tmean/ΔT from 2009–2013. |
| climate_zone_context | Method performed less well in the climatically heterogeneous Espírito Santo (r² lower than Vanderlinden's Spain results), but method captures HC variation tied to mean temperature and diurnal amplitude. |
| target_variable_definition | Targets the HC coefficient used to scale HS; HC computed daily as HC = 0.0023 * (ET0_PM / ET0_HS) and averaged per station for regression fitting. |
| predictors_used | Station mean ratio Tmean/ΔT (Tmean divided by thermal amplitude) as sole predictor in the canonical Vanderlinden formulation; other approaches (Martí) extend predictors. |
| fao56_assumption_details | Not specifically FAO-56; method is a regionalization for HS coefficient, used in conjunction with HS which can serve as FAO alternative. |
| model_family | Simple linear regression (HC as linear function of Tmean/ΔT). |
| localization_strategy | Regional regression across stations using station means (i.e., create one regional HC model for the study region). Evaluation in this paper used same data as fit (authors followed Vanderlinden's approach). |
| seasonality_handling | HC computed as station mean (averaging across season/day); no DOY decomposition. |
| day_of_year_window | None. |
| anomaly_definition | None. |
| autoregressive_or_lagged_terms | None. |
| physical_mechanisms_for_skill | Rationale: Tmean/ΔT ratio summarizes climatic regime (e.g., lower ΔT or higher Tmean associated with more humid/cloudy conditions) that modulates the HC required to match HS to PM. |
| interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling | Not explicitly discussed; method essentially collapses seasonal/DOY variability into station mean HC, assuming station climatology captures the dominant signal. |
| validation_data_sources | HC derived from PM reference ET0 and HS ET0 (daily), then averaged per station; regional regression coefficients estimated and reported (Eq. 11: HC = 0.00004 * Tmean/ΔT + 0.00011 in this study). |
| performance_metrics | Vanderlinden approach aggregated: MAE = 0.77 mm day⁻¹, MBE = 0.17, RMSE = 1.00 mm day⁻¹, RRMSE = 0.27, r² = 0.54 (lower than in Vanderlinden's original Spain results where r²≈0.90). |
| comparators_and_baselines | Compared against original HS, Martí HC models, PML, and linear regression correction. Vanderlinden performed better than PML but worse than simple global linear regression correction in this region. |
| reported_failure_modes | Fit quality degraded in a heterogeneous climatic region; lower r² suggests the single predictor Tmean/ΔT insufficient to capture HC variability across the diverse climates in Espírito Santo. |
| unphysical_dewpoint_extremes | Not applicable/Not reported. |
| mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias | Not discussed. |
| constraints_and_physical_plausibility_checks | None reported beyond ordinary regression diagnostics; authors compared coefficient magnitudes with Vanderlinden's original study. |
| data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues | Authors note that Vanderlinden's stronger results in Spain likely stem from climate homogeneity there; in Espírito Santo heterogeneity and limited station sample degrade regression performance. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Fig. 2 (HC dispersion vs Tmean/ΔT), Eq. 11 (fitted Vanderlinden relation), Table 3 (performance comparison). |

content.title: Martí et al. (2015) method for HC adjustment using temperature and geographic variables

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Martí et al. (2015) HC multiple regression |
| name_full | Martí et al. (2015) method for HC adjustment using temperature and geographic variables |
| brief_description | Multiple linear regression approach to estimate HC from available station descriptors (Tmean, ΔT, latitude, longitude, altitude) enabling a regional HC model that uses easily accessible geographic inputs. |
| citation_title |  |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region | Martí-style models were fit to station mean HC across the Espírito Santo network; several model variants (1–8) combining temperature and geographic predictors were tested. |
| climate_zone_context | Tested across the state's varied climates; inclusion of geographic coordinates provided little improvement in this heterogeneous region compared to temperature-only models. |
| target_variable_definition | Predict HC (Hargreaves coefficient) to scale HS ET0 to PM reference. |
| predictors_used | Tmean, ΔT (base); optional latitude (τ), longitude (φ), altitude (z) included in different model variants. Example Model 7 in this study: HC = 7.00e-4 + 3.46e-5 Tmean - 1.13e-4 ΔT - 3.91e-5 φ - 1.10e-7 z (units as in paper). |
| fao56_assumption_details | Not directly FAO-56; this is HC regionalization to improve HS (an FAO-recommended temperature-only alternative). |
| model_family | Multiple linear regression (station-mean HC regressed on station covariates). |
| localization_strategy | Regional across all stations; models produce a regional mapping from geography/temperature stats to HC enabling application at ungauged locations with known coordinates/altitude/temperature climatology. |
| seasonality_handling | HC derived from station mean HC aggregated over 5-year record; no DOY-specific calibration. |
| day_of_year_window | None. |
| anomaly_definition | None. |
| autoregressive_or_lagged_terms | None. |
| physical_mechanisms_for_skill | Motivation: geographic variables capture regional climatological influences (coastal vs interior, altitude, latitude/longitude gradients) on the Tmin–Tdew/radiation relationship and thus on HC. |
| interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling | Not explicitly discussed; station-mean approach assumes climatological station characteristics encapsulate seasonal effects sufficiently for HC estimation. |
| validation_data_sources | HC computed from PM reference ET0 and HS ET0; multiple linear regressions fit to station-mean HC values. Table 2 reports model coefficients and fit metrics (RRMSE ~0.046–0.048, r² ~0.53–0.56). |
| performance_metrics | Best Martí model in study (model 7) gave RRMSE=0.046, r²=0.56, MAE (HC) ~7e-5 (dimensionless). When propagated to ET0, Martí aggregate ET0 performance: MAE=0.81 mm day⁻¹, MBE=-0.18, RMSE=1.01, RRMSE=0.27, r²=0.54. |
| comparators_and_baselines | Compared to Vanderlinden HC, original HS and linear regression ET0 correction. Martí models performed similarly to Vanderlinden in this dataset and worse than the global linear regression correction. |
| reported_failure_modes | Geographic covariates provided little improvement over temperature-only model in Espírito Santo (unlike Martí's results in eastern Spain), attributed to climate heterogeneity and limited sample size. |
| unphysical_dewpoint_extremes | Not applicable/Not reported. |
| mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias | Not discussed. |
| constraints_and_physical_plausibility_checks | None reported beyond regression performance metrics. |
| data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues | Authors note models may be limited by only five years of data and by the heterogeneity across stations; Martí's superior results in Spain likely due to regional homogeneity which is lacking here. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Table 2 (Martí model coefficients and fit statistics), Table 3 (propagated ET0 performance), Table 4 (site-level best/worst where Martí model performed). |

content.title: Global linear regression calibration of HS ET0 to PM ET0 (ET0 = a + b * ET0_HS)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Linear regression ET0 correction |
| name_full | Global linear regression calibration of HS ET0 to PM ET0 (ET0 = a + b * ET0_HS) |
| brief_description | A simple linear regression of PM ET0 against HS ET0 fit on pooled daily data produced a multiplicative and additive correction (ET0 = 1.08 * ET0_HS - 0.81), which reduced bias and overall error relative to other tested calibrations. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region | Fitted using pooled daily data from the 16/17 stations in Espírito Santo region for 2009–2013; evaluated with leave-one-out cross-validation so each station's evaluation used coefficients fit without that station's data. |
| climate_zone_context | Applied across all climates in the region; produced overall best aggregated performance but station-level performance varied (best in Serra dos Aimorés, worst in Presidente Kennedy). |
| target_variable_definition | Corrects HS-derived ET0 to match PM reference ET0; does not directly estimate dew point or vapor pressure but empirically corrects HS output that depends on Tmin/Tmax. |
| predictors_used | Single predictor ET0_HS (daily HS output). |
| fao56_assumption_details | Not an FAO procedure — this is a statistical post-hoc correction of HS using PM as reference. It implicitly adjusts for systematic biases including those due to Tmin→Tdew mis-specification in PML or HS radiation proxy errors. |
| model_family | Ordinary least squares linear regression; evaluated with leave-one-out cross-validation for station-level assessment. |
| localization_strategy | Global/regional single regression fitted across all stations but evaluated in a cross-validated (leave-one-out) manner to approximate out-of-sample performance. |
| seasonality_handling | None explicit — coefficients are constant year-round (no DOY stratification). |
| day_of_year_window | None. |
| anomaly_definition | None. |
| autoregressive_or_lagged_terms | None. |
| physical_mechanisms_for_skill | Statistical correction captures average systematic offsets in HS (e.g., due to humidity/radiation biases) across pooled conditions; authors note it changes slope and intercept without changing dispersion (so r² unchanged but bias removed). |
| interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling | Authors used pooled daily data to estimate a single correction; they argue this is easily applied and performed best among tested methods, but they also recommend future work with day/condition-specific calibrations (Zanetti et al. 2019) for further improvement. |
| validation_data_sources | PM ET0 with full data used as target; regression coefficients reported (ET0 = 1.08 ET0_HS - 0.81) with r² = 0.78 (p < 0.01). Leave-one-out cross-validation used for station-level evaluation. |
| performance_metrics | Linear regression aggregated performance: MAE = 0.53 mm day⁻¹, MBE ≈ 0.00, RMSE = 0.68 mm day⁻¹, RRMSE = 0.18, r² = 0.78. Improved MAE by up to ~30% relative to original HS. |
| comparators_and_baselines | Outperformed original HS, Vanderlinden HC and Martí HC adjustments, and PML in aggregated metrics for this region. |
| reported_failure_modes | Although best on average, linear regression underperformed at some individual sites where it produced underestimation (e.g., Presidente Kennedy had MAE 0.78 mm day⁻¹ and MBE -0.60). Authors caution that longer series and site-specific calibrations could further improve results. |
| unphysical_dewpoint_extremes | Not applicable/Not reported. |
| mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias | Not discussed. |
| constraints_and_physical_plausibility_checks | No explicit physical constraints applied to corrected ET0 (correction purely statistical). |
| data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues | Authors used leave-one-out cross-validation to mitigate overfitting to stations; still emphasize the benefit of longer records and more stations for robust calibration. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Eq. 12 (ET0 = 1.08 ET0_HS - 0.81), Fig. 3e and Fig. 4 (scatter before/after correction), Table 3 (aggregated performance), Table 4 (site-level best/worst). |

metadata.title: Modelling weather data by approximate regression quantiles.

tldr.text: The present paper extends approximate quantile functionals onto parametric models and call them approximate regression quantiles and obtains five-curve summaries of the varying over time probability distributions of the considered weather components.

content.title: Approximate regression quantiles (based on M-functionals with correction)

content.text:
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| name_short | Approx. regression quantiles |
| name_full | Approximate regression quantiles (based on M-functionals with correction) |
| brief_description | A method that fits parametric diurnal regression curves using M-functionals (Huber M-function) and applies a variance-based shrinkage correction to produce approximate conditional p-quantile curves (p = 0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95) of weather variables as functions of time of day and month. |
| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| study_region | Automatic Weather Station, Macquarie University (Sydney, Australia); four years of local AWS data (1994–1997) recorded at 15-minute intervals. No broader geographic coordinates or elevation ranges are provided in the paper. |
| climate_zone_context | Not explicitly classified in the paper; only the AWS at Macquarie University is specified. The paper does not discuss humid tropical lowlands, Amazon, or dry-season transitions. |
| target_variable_definition | The paper models several weather components (global radiation, wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, soil temperature, soil heat flux). The method is applied to wet-bulb temperature and relative humidity among others; dew-point temperature (Td), actual vapor pressure, or specific humidity are not explicitly modeled or reconstructed in this paper. |
| predictors_used | Primary predictor is time of day (X) within a month; models are parametric functions of time (cosine functions for temperature, RH, wet-bulb; polynomial-type daytime functions for radiation; max(constant, cosine) for wind). Tmin is not used as a predictor for reconstructing dew point in this paper and FAO-56 assumptions are not discussed. |
| fao56_assumption_details | null |
| model_family | Parametric diurnal regression models combined with robust M-estimation (M-functionals). Specifically: cosine-based parametric models for 24-hour variables (Y = A*cos(pi*(X+B)/12) + C + eps), polynomial-type daylight models for radiation, and special max-constant/cosine form for wind; estimation via empirical M-function minimization with Huber M-function (s = 1). The approximate quantiles are produced by applying a correction factor (kappa) to regression M-functionals. |
| localization_strategy | Seasonal/monthly localization: models are fitted separately for each month (the paper refers to 'typical for a given month' and fits curves for each of 48 months in the 4-year record). No per-station-vs-gridcell strategy is discussed beyond using the single AWS station. |
| seasonality_handling | Monthly models (parametric diurnal curve fitted for each month). The method therefore accounts for seasonality by separate month-specific model fits; within-month diurnal variation is modeled explicitly by the parametric form. |
| day_of_year_window | Implicit monthly pooling (i.e., data pooled per calendar month across years). No explicit day-of-year window lengths like 30/45 days are reported and no alternative DOY-window experiments are described. |
| anomaly_definition | No anomaly definitions are provided; the method models absolute values conditional on time-of-day and month (no explicit detrending or anomaly-based predictors are used). |
| autoregressive_or_lagged_terms | None reported. The models do not include lagged dew point/humidity or autoregressive terms. |
| physical_mechanisms_for_skill | The paper gives general diurnal/phenomenological explanations (e.g., daily minimum typically occurs just before sunrise and maximum in mid-afternoon), and notes heteroscedasticity of weather variables and the effect of cloud/diurnal cycle on variance. It does not provide mechanistic discussion specific to Tmin→Td coupling, nocturnal boundary-layer moisture coupling, or moisture advection processes. |
| interpretation_of_wide_doy_pooling | The paper uses month-based pooling; the implicit rationale is parsimony and capturing a 'typical' monthly diurnal pattern while using limited-parameter models. It also remarks that use of convex M-functions and the correction reduces variance of estimators, suggesting a trade-off between variance and bias, but it does not explicitly analyze DOY-window width choices or provide a formal statistical justification for monthly pooling vs narrower/wider windows. |
| validation_data_sources | Validation/illustration uses the same AWS station data (15-minute measurements aggregated or plotted on daily/monthly scales) from Macquarie University (1994–1997). No independent radiosonde, flux-tower, reanalysis, or satellite validation datasets are used or reported. |
| performance_metrics | No standard error metrics (RMSE/MAE/R2) are reported for dew point or humidity reconstruction. The paper reports qualitative/check metrics: designed so approximately 5% of observed values lie below the 5% curve and 5% above the 95% curve; the shrinkage correction parameter kappa is reported numerically in examples (e.g., kappa = 0.8325 for wind speed example). Variance estimator used: sigma^2 estimated as mean squared residuals from median fit. No seasonal/regime breakdown of numeric skill scores is provided. |
| comparators_and_baselines | Main methodological comparison is between uncorrected regression M-quantiles (regression M-functionals) and the corrected approximate regression quantiles (with shrinkage factor kappa). For wind speed the paper shows that uncorrected M-quantiles produce overly wide separation and do not leave ~5% of data below the 5% curve, whereas corrected approximate quantiles restore expected coverage. No comparison against FAO-56, Tmin-based methods, persistence, climatology, or reanalysis is performed. |
| reported_failure_modes | The main failure mode reported is that uncorrected regression M-functionals (i.e., without the variance shrinkage correction) can produce substantially inflated conditional-quantile spreads so that the nominal coverage is violated (example: wind speed where no observed points fall below the 5% M-quantile). Instrument censoring (anemometer records low wind speeds between 0 and 0.2 m/s as 0.2 m/s) is identified as a data/mechanism-specific complication that can distort quantile fits if not modeled explicitly. The paper cautions that not using the correction (17) 'may obtain results significantly departing from any sensible modelling of conditional quantiles.' |
| unphysical_dewpoint_extremes | No mentions. The paper does not report unphysical dew-point values, RH>100% issues, or extremely high dew points in humid tropical lowlands; dew point estimation from Tmin and FAO-56-style failures are not discussed. |
| mechanisms_for_late_dry_season_bias | None reported. The paper does not discuss tropical dry-season transitions, biomass burning effects, moisture recycling, or related mechanisms. |
| constraints_and_physical_plausibility_checks | Two pragmatic checks are described: (1) the shrinkage correction kappa (kappa = sqrt(sigma^2/(sigma^2 + Var(G)))) is applied to regression M-functionals to reduce inflated spread and better match nominal quantile coverage; (2) for wind speed the model enforces a lower bound (an explicit max{...,0.2}) to mimic instrument censoring. There are no explicit general physical constraints for humidity/dew point (e.g., Td <= T or RH clipping) discussed in the paper. |
| data_sparsity_and_sampling_issues | The paper uses four years of high-frequency data but does not analyze station-network sparsity; it mentions that convex M-functions combined with the correction can reduce estimator variance and improve numerical stability, implying attention to small-sample variance issues, but does not provide formal sampling diagnostics. Monthly pooling across years is used to increase sample size per-month fit. |
| key_figures_or_tables | Figure 1 (global radiation first 72 hours, with regression quantiles), Figure 2 (global radiation for January with five regression quantile curves), Figure 3 (wet-bulb temperature with regression quantiles), Figure 4 (midday regression quantiles for global radiation over 48 months), Figure 5 (wind speed in August 1994: above shows uncorrected regression M-quantiles, below shows approximate regression quantiles after correction). |
